options.text: Never remove it for skin care
Remove it as allowed by orders to inspect the skin, keep it snug but not tight, and check circulation and sensation in the foot
Tighten it until the leg is numb
Wear it over wet clothing

questions.stem: A client says, "I'm the president, and the FBI is trying to capture me." Which response by the LPN/VN is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Arguing with or exploring a delusion in detail reinforces it. Responding to the underlying feeling and redirecting to reality-based activities is therapeutic.

options.text: "You're not the president."
"That sounds frightening. You're safe here. Let's go get some lunch."
"Tell me more about being president."
"How do you know the FBI is after you?"

questions.stem: A caregiver reports feeling constantly stressed. Which healthy coping strategies should the LPN/VN suggest?
questions.rationale: Healthy coping strategies reduce stress and improve well-being. The nurse also watches for signs of depression or burnout.

options.text: Increasing alcohol use to relax
Regular physical activity, adequate sleep, relaxation techniques, time for enjoyable activities, and seeking support
Skipping meals
Isolating from friends

questions.stem: A pregnant client reports a stuffy nose and occasional nosebleeds. Which response by the LPN/VN is appropriate?
questions.rationale: Increased blood volume and estrogen cause mucosal swelling. Frequent or heavy nosebleeds should be reported. Decongestant sprays can cause rebound congestion.

options.text: "This means you have a serious infection."
"Pregnancy hormones increase blood flow to the nose, so congestion and minor nosebleeds are common. A humidifier and saline spray may help. Check with your provider before taking decongestants."
"Use decongestant nasal spray several times a day for weeks."
"Pick your nose to clear it."

questions.stem: A client who had an uncomplicated vaginal birth 3 days ago asks about exercise. Which suggestion should the LPN/VN offer?
questions.rationale: Gradual return to activity supports recovery, mood, and circulation. More strenuous exercise is resumed as healing allows. Heavy bleeding or pain signals the need to slow down.

options.text: "Start running 5 miles daily this week."
"Begin with gentle activity such as walking and pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, and gradually increase as you feel ready and your provider advises."
"Don't move for 6 weeks."
"Do heavy sit-ups today."

questions.stem: A parent worries that the newborn is scratching the face with long nails. Which suggestion should the LPN/VN offer?
questions.rationale: Filing is gentle and reduces the risk of cutting the skin. Biting nails can introduce infection.

options.text: "Bite the nails off."
"Gently file the nails with a soft emery board, or trim them carefully with baby clippers when the baby is asleep. Soft mittens can be used briefly."
"Tape the hands down."
"Use adult nail clippers while the baby is awake and moving."

questions.stem: A hospitalized toddler has RSV. Which precautions should the LPN/VN follow?
questions.rationale: RSV spreads mainly by direct contact with secretions and contaminated surfaces, as well as by large droplets. It survives on surfaces for hours, so hand hygiene and cleaning are critical.

options.text: Airborne precautions only
Contact precautions (and droplet precautions per facility policy), with a gown and gloves, and strict hand hygiene
No precautions are needed
Neutropenic precautions

questions.stem: A client with severe low vision is going home. Which home safety suggestion should the LPN/VN offer?
questions.rationale: Consistency, contrast, and good lighting help people with low vision move safely. Medications can be labeled with large print or tactile markers.

options.text: "Rearrange your furniture often."
"Keep furniture and items in consistent places, use high-contrast tape on step edges, add bright even lighting, and remove clutter."
"Keep lights dim to reduce glare."
"Store medications in similar containers."

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is a normal newborn reflex finding or should be reported.
questions.rationale: Primitive reflexes are expected in newborns and fade on schedule. A weak suck may signal prematurity, illness, or neurological problems. An asymmetric Moro suggests injury such as a clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury, and persistence beyond the expected age suggests a neurological problem.
questions.answer_summary: Normal: rooting, symmetric Moro, positive Babinski in a newborn. Report: weak or absent suck, asymmetric Moro, persistent Moro at 9 months.

rows.text: Rooting when the cheek is stroked
Toes fan out when the sole is stroked (Babinski) in a newborn
Moro reflex present on one side only
Moro reflex still present at 9 months of age

questions.stem: A resident started a new antihypertensive today. When standing to walk to the bathroom, the resident says, "I'm dizzy and everything is going gray." BP lying was 128/78 mm Hg; standing it is 94/60 mm Hg with HR 104/min. Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the resident is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.rationale: A systolic drop of 20 mm Hg or more on standing, with symptoms after a new antihypertensive, indicates orthostatic hypotension, a major fall risk in older adults. The provider may adjust the medication. Slow position changes and hydration help.
questions.answer_summary: Condition: orthostatic hypotension. Actions: sit or lie the resident down immediately; report findings and the new medication to the RN. Monitor: orthostatic vital signs; dizziness and fall risk.

bowtie_groups.label: Actions to take (choose 2)
options: Help the resident sit or lie down immediately to prevent a fall
Report the findings and the new medication to the RN
Encourage the resident to walk faster to the bathroom
Give the next dose of the antihypertensive early
Leave the resident standing to adjust

bowtie_groups.label: Parameters to monitor (choose 2)
options: Lying and standing BP and heart rate
Dizziness and fall risk during position changes

questions.stem: A breastfed infant has white patches in the mouth that don't wipe off, and the mother has sore, shiny, pink nipples. Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce?
questions.rationale: Candida passes back and forth between the infant's mouth and the mother's nipples. Treating both and sanitizing objects prevents reinfection.

options.text: "Treat only the baby."
"Both you and your baby may need antifungal treatment, and pacifiers and pump parts should be cleaned or boiled daily."
"Stop breastfeeding permanently."
"This is breast milk residue."

questions.stem: A parent asks how long a time-out should last for a 3-year-old. Which guideline should the LPN/VN share?
questions.rationale: Short, consistent time-outs are effective discipline for young children. They are paired with praise for positive behavior.

options.text: "30 minutes."
"About 1 minute per year of age, so about 3 minutes, in a safe, boring spot."
"Until the child apologizes, no matter how long."
"An hour in a dark room."

questions.stem: A parent says the 6-year-old has leg aches at night. Which finding should the LPN/VN report as not typical of growing pains?
questions.rationale: Growing pains are usually in both legs, occur at night, and do not affect daytime activity. One-sided pain, a limp, fever, or systemic symptoms need evaluation for infection, injury, or tumor.

options.text: Aching in both legs in the evening that is gone by morning
Pain in one leg with limping, swelling, fever, or pain that wakes the child and continues into the day
Pain relieved by massage
Normal activity during the day

questions.stem: The LPN/VN is screening a 12-year-old for scoliosis. Which technique is used?
questions.rationale: A rib hump or uneven shoulders or hips on forward bending suggests scoliosis and prompts referral.

options.text: Have the child lie flat and measure leg length
Have the child bend forward at the waist with arms hanging down, and look for asymmetry of the ribs or back (Adams forward bend test)
Check reflexes only
Have the child walk on tiptoes

questions.stem: Which intervention helps prevent skin tears in a frail older resident?
questions.rationale: Aging skin is thin and fragile. Moisture, padding, protective clothing, and gentle handling reduce tears.

options.text: Use adhesive tape directly on the skin
Keep skin moisturized, pad bed rails and wheelchair parts, encourage long sleeves, and use lift sheets rather than pulling on the arms
Rub the skin vigorously when drying
Keep fingernails long

questions.stem: A client on bed rest needs hair care. Which action by the LPN/VN is appropriate?
questions.rationale: Hair care supports hygiene and dignity. Products for bed shampooing make it safe and comfortable. Neck position is supported.

options.text: Wait until the client is discharged
Use a shampoo cap or rinse-free shampoo, or a shampoo basin with warm water, protect the bed, and dry the hair well
Use very hot water
Cut the client's hair without permission

questions.stem: A client's order after ankle surgery reads "toe-touch weight bearing" on the operative leg. What does this mean?
questions.rationale: Weight-bearing orders range from non-weight-bearing and toe-touch to partial, as-tolerated, and full weight bearing. Assistive devices and teaching must match the order to protect the repair.

options.text: The client may put full weight on the leg
The client may touch the toes to the floor for balance but should not put weight through the leg
The client may not touch the floor at all
The client can bear weight as tolerated

questions.stem: A client has a new fever on postoperative day 5. Which cause should the LPN/VN recognize as common at this time?
questions.rationale: The "5 W's" help identify postoperative fever causes: wind (lungs), water (urine), wound, walking (DVT), and wonder drugs. Timing helps identify the likely source.

options.text: Fever on day 5 is never significant
Wound infection, urinary tract infection, or deep vein thrombosis
Normal inflammatory response only
Anesthesia reaction

questions.stem: How does buccal administration differ from sublingual administration?
questions.rationale: Both routes absorb medication through the oral mucosa and bypass first-pass metabolism. The client should not eat, drink, or chew until the medication has dissolved.

options.text: Buccal medications are swallowed
Buccal medications are placed between the cheek and gum to dissolve, while sublingual medications are placed under the tongue
They are the same
Buccal medications are chewed

questions.stem: A medication is scheduled for 0900. Many facilities allow a window for routine scheduled medications. What is a common window for non-time-critical medications?
questions.rationale: Following policy-defined windows ensures consistent drug levels. Time-critical medications, such as some antibiotics, insulin, and Parkinson's drugs, have tighter windows.

options.text: Any time during the shift
Within about 1 hour before or after the scheduled time, per facility policy
Only exactly at 0900
Within 4 hours

questions.stem: A client with seasonal pollen allergies asks how to reduce symptoms at home. Which suggestion should the LPN/VN offer?
questions.rationale: Reducing exposure to pollen helps control allergic rhinitis alongside prescribed medications.

options.text: "Open all windows on windy days."
"Keep windows closed during high pollen times, use air conditioning, shower and change clothes after being outdoors, and check pollen forecasts."
"Hang laundry outside to dry."
"Mow the lawn daily."

questions.stem: A client with high LDL cholesterol asks about diet. Which choice should the LPN/VN recommend?
questions.rationale: Limiting saturated and trans fats and increasing soluble fiber lower LDL. A Mediterranean-style pattern supports heart health.

options.text: Fried foods and fatty red meat daily
Foods rich in fiber, such as oats, beans, fruits, and vegetables, with fish, nuts, and olive oil in place of saturated fats
Butter and whole-fat cheese at every meal
Sugary drinks

questions.stem: A client who uses chewing tobacco has a white patch inside the cheek that hasn't healed for 3 weeks. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Leukoplakia and erythroplakia are potential precursors of oral cancer. Sores lasting more than 2 weeks need evaluation. Tobacco and alcohol are major risk factors.

options.text: Tell the client it's normal
Report the finding for evaluation, because a persistent white or red patch can be precancerous, and encourage tobacco cessation
Apply mouthwash and recheck in a year
Scrape it off

questions.stem: A client is alarmed that their urine is reddish after eating beets at dinner. There is no pain, and the client is otherwise well. What should the LPN/VN say?
questions.rationale: Some foods and medications, such as beets, rifampin, and phenazopyridine, change urine color. Persistent red urine is tested for blood to rule out hematuria.

options.text: "This definitely means kidney cancer."
"Beets can turn urine pink or red. If it continues after you stop eating them, or you have other symptoms, it should be checked for blood."
"Stop drinking water."
"Red urine is always normal."

questions.stem: A resident with moderate dementia has trouble finding clothes and the bathroom. Which intervention should the LPN/VN suggest?
questions.rationale: Visual cues and a consistent environment support independence and reduce confusion and incontinence.

options.text: Rearrange the room weekly
Label drawers and doors with pictures and words, keep a consistent layout, and use a night-light for the bathroom
Remove all clocks and calendars
Keep the resident in bed

questions.stem: The LPN/VN notes that a client's fingertips are enlarged and the angle between the nail and nail bed is increased. Which condition is associated with this finding?
questions.rationale: Clubbing develops over time with chronic hypoxia and some other conditions. It is documented and reported, especially if new.

options.text: Acute sprain
Chronic hypoxemia, such as from long-term lung disease or congenital heart disease
Recent sunburn
Dehydration

questions.stem: A client who had a total knee replacement 3 weeks ago calls reporting increasing knee pain, redness, warmth, drainage, and fever. What should the LPN/VN advise?
questions.rationale: Prosthetic joint infection is serious and may require surgery and long-term antibiotics. Early evaluation improves outcomes.

options.text: "This is normal healing."
"Contact your surgeon today for evaluation, because these may be signs of an infection in the new joint."
"Apply heat and wait a week."
"Take leftover antibiotics."

questions.stem: A client has an intense fear of needles that prevents needed blood tests. Which treatment approach is commonly effective?
questions.rationale: Gradual, controlled exposure paired with coping skills reduces phobic responses. For needle phobia with fainting, applied tension techniques can also help.

options.text: Avoiding all medical care
Gradual exposure (systematic desensitization) combined with relaxation techniques, often guided by a therapist
Forcing the client to have many blood draws at once
Telling the client to "just get over it"

questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks' gestation reports feeling short of breath when climbing stairs. There is no chest pain, cough, or swelling, and vital signs are normal. How should the LPN/VN respond?
questions.rationale: Mild exertional dyspnea is common in late pregnancy. Sudden or severe dyspnea may indicate pulmonary embolism or peripartum cardiomyopathy and needs prompt evaluation.

options.text: "You are having a heart attack."

"The growing uterus pushes up on your diaphragm, so mild breathlessness is common. It often eases when the baby drops before labor. Report chest pain, sudden or severe shortness of breath, or coughing up blood."
"Stop all activity until delivery."
"Lie flat on your back to breathe better."

questions.stem: The LPN/VN checks a postpartum pad after 1 hour and finds a stain larger than 6 inches that saturates most of the pad. How should the nurse document the lochia?
questions.rationale: Common descriptions are scant (under 1 inch), light (under 4 inches), moderate (under 6 inches), and heavy (saturated pad within 1 hour). Heavy bleeding requires assessment for hemorrhage.

options.text: Scant
Heavy, which should be reported
Light
Normal

questions.stem: Which technique should the LPN/VN use when giving a newborn a sponge bath?
questions.rationale: Wiping from inner to outer prevents carrying debris into the tear duct. Exposing and drying one area at a time prevents heat loss.

options.text: Use soap on the eyes
Clean each eye with plain water from the inner to the outer corner using a clean part of the cloth, then wash the face, and keep the baby warm, washing and drying one area at a time
Immerse the newborn in water before the cord falls off
Bathe in a cool room

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 5-year-old was exposed to measles 2 days ago at a clinic. What should the LPN/VN expect the provider to recommend?
questions.rationale: Post-exposure prophylaxis can prevent or lessen measles. Exposed susceptible people may be excluded from school and other settings during the incubation period.

options.text: No action is needed
The MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure (or immune globulin within 6 days if the vaccine is not appropriate), and monitoring for symptoms
Antibiotics
An antiviral for influenza

questions.stem: Which bathroom safety measure should the LPN/VN ensure for a resident at risk for falls?
questions.rationale: Many falls occur in bathrooms. Accessible call lights, grab bars, nonslip surfaces, and supervision reduce risk. Doors are not locked so staff can reach the resident quickly.

options.text: Remove the call light from the bathroom
Make sure the call light is within reach, use nonslip mats and grab bars, and stay nearby if the resident needs help
Leave wet towels on the floor
Lock the bathroom door

questions.stem: For each term or instruction, indicate its meaning.
questions.rationale: Understanding timing terms prevents errors. Many facilities discourage abbreviations like "hs" and prefer the full words (such as "bedtime") to reduce misinterpretation.
questions.answer_summary: Before meals: ac, 30 minutes before breakfast. After meals: pc, after dinner. At bedtime: hs. As needed: prn.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old comes to the school health office with pain that began near the belly button this morning and has moved to the lower right abdomen. The student has vomited once, has a temperature of 100.8°F (38.2°C), and walks bent forward. Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the student is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.rationale: Pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant, with nausea, low-grade fever, and guarding, suggests appendicitis. The student may need surgery, so food and drink are withheld. Laxatives and heat can increase the risk of perforation, and sudden pain relief may signal rupture.
questions.answer_summary: Condition: suspected appendicitis. Actions: keep NPO; notify parents and arrange urgent evaluation. Monitor: changes in pain; temperature and vital signs.

bowtie_groups.label: Actions to take (choose 2)
options: Keep the student NPO (nothing to eat or drink)
Notify the parents and arrange urgent medical evaluation
Apply a heating pad to the abdomen
Give ibuprofen and send the student back to class

bowtie_groups.label: Parameters to monitor (choose 2)
options: Changes in pain, including sudden relief followed by worsening

questions.stem: A parent reports that the 18-month-old sometimes cries hard, holds the breath, turns blue, and briefly goes limp before breathing again. The child's exam is normal. What should the LPN/VN explain?
questions.rationale: Breath-holding spells are involuntary and usually harmless. Iron deficiency is associated with them. Spells lasting more than a minute or with prolonged jerking need evaluation.

options.text: "This is always a seizure disorder."

"Breath-holding spells are common in toddlers and usually outgrown. Stay calm, place your child on their side for safety, and avoid rewarding the behavior. Tell the provider, who may check for iron deficiency."
"Shake your child to restart breathing."
"Splash cold water on your child's face."

questions.stem: A 3-year-old who was toilet trained begins having accidents after a new baby arrives. What should the LPN/VN tell the parents?
questions.rationale: Stress and changes in attention can cause regression. Reassurance and attention help. Persistent problems, pain, or other symptoms should be evaluated.

options.text: "Punish your child for accidents."
"Temporary regression is common when a sibling is born. Avoid punishment, give your child special one-on-one time, and praise successes."
"Your child needs medication."
"Stop toilet training permanently."

questions.stem: A 9-year-old reports frequent headaches after school, squints at the board, and has trouble reading. What should the LPN/VN recommend?
questions.rationale: Refractive errors commonly cause headaches in children. Red flags such as morning vomiting, worsening pattern, or neurological signs require medical evaluation.

options.text: "Give pain relievers every day."
"Schedule a vision exam, because an uncorrected vision problem can cause headaches and eye strain."
"Limit water intake."
"Ignore the headaches."

questions.stem: A 16-year-old cross-country runner has lost weight, has missed three menstrual periods, and recently had a stress fracture. What should the LPN/VN recognize?
questions.rationale: Inadequate energy intake for training demands disrupts hormones and bone health. Early identification and nutritional support prevent long-term bone loss.

options.text: These are expected effects of training
These may indicate the female athlete triad (relative energy deficiency in sport): low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone density, and should be reported
The missed periods are a sign of good fitness
Stress fractures are unrelated to diet

questions.stem: A resident spends most of the day alone in a quiet room and has become withdrawn and less oriented. Which intervention should the LPN/VN suggest?
questions.rationale: Sensory deprivation contributes to withdrawal and confusion. Meaningful engagement and sensory aids support cognition and mood.

options.text: Keep the room dark and quiet all day
Encourage participation in meaningful activities, such as music, conversation, and group programs, and keep glasses and hearing aids in use
Discourage family visits
Leave the television on all night

questions.stem: Why should the LPN/VN palpate the radial pulse while inflating the BP cuff to estimate systolic pressure before auscultating?
questions.rationale: Inflating to about 20–30 mm Hg above the point where the radial pulse disappears ensures that the true systolic pressure is heard. Auscultatory gaps are more common in older adults with hypertension.

options.text: To save time
To avoid missing an auscultatory gap, a silent period that can cause the systolic pressure to be underestimated
To measure the diastolic pressure
It is not recommended

questions.stem: When taking a rectal temperature on a young infant (if permitted by policy), how far should the LPN/VN insert the lubricated thermometer?
questions.rationale: Shallow insertion prevents rectal injury. Many facilities prefer axillary or temporal methods for screening and use rectal temperatures for accuracy in young infants.

options.text: About 2 inches
About 1/2 inch (no more than about 1 inch)
As far as it will go
Just touching the skin outside

questions.stem: Which action is correct when the LPN/VN helps a client transfer from bed to wheelchair with a slide board?
questions.rationale: Slide boards help clients with good upper body strength transfer safely. Locked surfaces and proper board placement prevent falls.

options.text: Place the wheelchair far from the bed
Lock the wheelchair and bed, remove the wheelchair armrest next to the bed, place the board under the client's thigh, and have the client slide across in short movements
Lift the client over the board
Leave the wheels unlocked

questions.stem: An unconscious client is found to be wearing soft contact lenses. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Lenses left in can cause corneal injury and infection. Tap water can carry harmful organisms. Personal items are safeguarded and documented.

options.text: Leave them in until the client wakes up
Remove the lenses per procedure (or report to the RN), store them in labeled containers with solution, and document
Throw the lenses away
Rinse the lenses in tap water and replace them

questions.topic: Taking medications on an empty stomach
questions.stem: A medication label says "take on an empty stomach." What should the LPN/VN tell the client?
questions.rationale: Food can reduce the absorption of some drugs. Specific instructions for individual medications should be followed.

options.text: "Take it with a large meal."
"Take it about 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating."
"Take it with milk."
"Take it right after breakfast."

questions.stem: How must controlled substances such as opioids be stored on a nursing unit?
questions.rationale: Federal and state regulations require secure storage and accountability for controlled substances to prevent diversion and harm.

options.text: In the unlocked medication room
In a secure, locked system (such as double-locked storage or an automated dispensing cabinet) with access limited to authorized staff and counts documented
In the nurse's pocket
At the client's bedside

questions.stem: A client uses a home nebulizer several times a day. Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce?
questions.rationale: Moist parts can grow bacteria that are then inhaled. Regular cleaning and drying prevent respiratory infections.

options.text: "Clean it once a month."
"Rinse the medication cup and mouthpiece after each use, let them air dry, and disinfect them regularly as the manufacturer instructs."
"Store it wet in a sealed bag."
"Share the mouthpiece with family."

questions.stem: A client taking aspirin and clopidogrel after a heart stent is scheduled for a dental procedure. What should the LPN/VN advise?
questions.rationale: Stopping antiplatelet therapy early can cause stent thrombosis. Most dental procedures can be done safely while continuing these medications.

options.text: "Stop both medications a week before."
"Tell your dentist about your medications and check with your cardiologist before stopping either one."
"Take extra doses before the procedure."
"These medications don't affect bleeding."

questions.stem: A client is starting psyllium for constipation. Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce?
questions.rationale: Without enough fluid, bulk laxatives can cause choking or bowel obstruction. They are separated from other medications to avoid reducing absorption.

options.text: "Take it with a small sip of water."
"Mix it with a full glass of water or other fluid, drink it right away, and drink plenty of fluids during the day."
"Take it dry."
"Take it at the same time as your other medications."

questions.stem: A client uses a urinary leg bag during the day. Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce?
questions.rationale: Proper placement and strap tension prevent backflow and skin or circulation problems. Larger night bags hold overnight output.

options.text: "Wear the leg bag straps as tight as possible."
"Keep the bag below the bladder, fasten the straps snugly but not tight enough to restrict circulation, empty it when about half full, and switch to a larger bedside bag at night."
"Wear the leg bag above your knee while lying down."
"Never empty the bag."

questions.stem: A resident who had a stroke suddenly laughs or cries uncontrollably in situations that don't match the emotion, then says, "I don't know why that happens." How should the LPN/VN respond?
questions.rationale: Pseudobulbar affect results from brain injury, not from the person's actual feelings. Understanding reduces embarrassment, and medications may help.

options.text: "Stop that right now."
Stay calm, explain to the resident and family that this can be a neurological effect of stroke, and use gentle distraction. Report it to the RN, since treatment is available.
Laugh along with the resident
Leave the room

questions.stem: Where should the LPN/VN check skin turgor in an older adult to get a more reliable result?
questions.rationale: Skin on the back of the hand loses elasticity with age and can give falsely poor turgor. Turgor is still only one part of a hydration assessment, along with mucous membranes, intake and output, and weight.

options.text: The back of the hand
The skin over the sternum or forehead
The earlobe
The palm

questions.stem: A client reports sharp heel pain with the first steps in the morning. Plantar fasciitis is diagnosed. Which suggestion should the LPN/VN offer?
questions.rationale: Stretching, supportive footwear, and icing reduce inflammation and pain. Most cases improve with conservative care.

options.text: "Walk barefoot on hard floors."
"Stretch your calf and the bottom of your foot before getting out of bed, wear supportive shoes, and roll your foot over a cold water bottle."
"Stop all walking permanently."
"Wear flat sandals without support."

questions.stem: At which level of anxiety is a client most able to learn new information?
questions.rationale: Mild anxiety increases alertness and motivation. As anxiety increases, perception narrows, and teaching becomes ineffective at severe and panic levels. Anxiety is reduced before teaching.

options.text: Mild anxiety
Severe anxiety
Panic
Anxiety has no effect on learning

questions.stem: A client is at 28 weeks' gestation. What fundal height does the LPN/VN expect?
questions.rationale: Between about 20 and 36 weeks, fundal height in centimeters roughly equals gestational age in weeks. Large differences may indicate growth problems or abnormal amniotic fluid and are reported.

options.text: About 14 cm
About 28 cm (within about 2 cm)
About 40 cm
About 10 cm

questions.stem: Which behavior by a new mother suggests healthy bonding?
questions.rationale: En face positioning, touch, talking, and responsiveness are signs of attachment. Concerning behaviors are reported so support can be provided.

options.text: Avoiding eye contact with the baby
Holding the baby face-to-face (en face position), talking to the baby, and responding to the baby's cues
Referring to the baby only as "it"
Declining to hold the baby at all times

questions.stem: Which action by the LPN/VN helps prevent infant abduction on a maternity unit?
questions.rationale: ID band matching, staff badges, security tags, and parent education are key parts of infant security programs.

options.text: Allowing anyone who asks to carry the newborn to the nursery
Matching the ID bands on the newborn and parent each time the baby is returned, and teaching parents to give the baby only to staff wearing proper identification
Leaving the newborn unattended in the hallway
Posting the newborn's name and photo on the door

questions.stem: A child with mumps is admitted for dehydration. Which precautions should the LPN/VN follow?
questions.rationale: Mumps spreads through respiratory droplets and saliva. MMR vaccination is the main prevention.

options.text: Airborne precautions
Droplet precautions (in addition to standard precautions) until about 5 days after the start of parotid gland swelling
No precautions are needed
Contact precautions only

questions.stem: For each behavior, indicate the postpartum maternal adjustment phase (Rubin) it best represents.
questions.rationale: In taking-in (first day or two), the mother is dependent and processes the birth. In taking-hold, she becomes independent and ready to learn, which makes it an ideal time for teaching. In letting-go, she integrates the new role. Timing varies.
questions.answer_summary: Taking-in: retelling the birth, focusing on own needs. Taking-hold: eager to learn baby care, many questions. Letting-go: accepting the new role, grieving the old one.

rows.text: Focuses on her own needs such as rest and food
Is eager to learn how to bathe the baby
Asks many questions about breastfeeding technique
Accepts her new role and adjusts family routines at home
Grieves the loss of her previous role and independence

questions.stem: A 70-year-old resident suddenly has slurred speech and right hand weakness while eating lunch. The symptoms resolve completely after 15 minutes, and the resident says, "I'm fine now." Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the resident most likely experienced, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.rationale: A TIA is a warning sign of stroke, with high risk in the following days. Urgent evaluation allows preventive treatment. Return of symptoms requires emergency response, and a fingerstick glucose may also be checked per protocol.
questions.answer_summary: Condition: TIA. Actions: report to the RN immediately for urgent evaluation; document timing and symptoms. Monitor: neurological status; BP.

bowtie_groups.label: Actions to take (choose 2)
options: Report the episode to the RN immediately for urgent evaluation, even though symptoms resolved
Document the time the symptoms began and ended and the specific symptoms
Tell the resident nothing needs to be done because they feel fine
Have the resident lie down and nap without notifying anyone

questions.stem: Which infant vomiting finding should parents report right away?
questions.rationale: Bilious vomiting can indicate intestinal obstruction, such as malrotation with volvulus, which is a surgical emergency. Projectile vomiting may suggest pyloric stenosis. Poor weight gain or dehydration also needs evaluation.

options.text: Small spit-ups after feedings in a thriving baby
Green (bile-stained) vomiting or forceful projectile vomiting
Spitting up when burped
Drooling

questions.stem: Which safety tip should the LPN/VN reinforce with parents to prevent child heatstroke in vehicles?
questions.rationale: Car interiors heat up quickly even on mild days, and children overheat faster than adults. Reminders and locked cars prevent tragedies.

options.text: "It's fine to leave a child in the car with the windows cracked."
"Never leave a child alone in a car, even briefly. Place an item you'll need, like your phone or bag, in the back seat as a reminder, and lock the car so kids can't get in."
"It only matters on very hot days."
"Air conditioning keeps a parked car safe for hours."

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has a dirty scrape on the knee from falling on a playground. What should the LPN/VN do first?
questions.rationale: Cleaning removes bacteria and debris. Harsh antiseptics damage tissue. Tetanus status is checked for dirty wounds.

options.text: Apply a bandage over the dirt
Wash the scrape gently with soap and clean running water to remove debris, then apply a clean dressing
Pour alcohol into the scrape
Leave it uncovered and dirty

questions.stem: A 16-year-old got a new ear cartilage piercing. Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce?
questions.rationale: Cartilage piercings heal slowly and are prone to infections that can damage the cartilage. Gentle saline care and avoiding contamination promote healing.

options.text: "Twist the jewelry often and remove it daily."
"Clean it with sterile saline as directed, avoid touching it with dirty hands, and report increasing redness, swelling, pus, or fever."
"Use alcohol and peroxide several times a day."
"Swim in lakes right away."

questions.stem: A frail resident is prescribed an oral nutritional supplement three times daily but is too full to finish meals. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Supplements given between meals add calories and protein without reducing appetite at meals. Intake is documented to track effectiveness.

options.text: Give the supplement right before meals
Offer the supplement between meals so it doesn't replace meal intake
Skip the supplement
Mix it into hot coffee

questions.stem: A client's BP is 120/60 mm Hg. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure (MAP)?
questions.rationale: MAP ≈ (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 = (120 + 120) ÷ 3 = 80 mm Hg. A MAP of at least about 65 mm Hg is generally needed to perfuse the organs.

options.text: 60 mm Hg
80 mm Hg
90 mm Hg
180 mm Hg

questions.stem: A client's BP is 150/60 mm Hg. What is the pulse pressure?
questions.rationale: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic (150 − 60 = 90 mm Hg). A normal pulse pressure is about 40 mm Hg. A widened pulse pressure can occur with aging arteries, aortic regurgitation, or increased ICP.

options.text: 60 mm Hg
90 mm Hg
150 mm Hg
210 mm Hg

questions.stem: A resident with missing teeth and poorly fitting dentures has trouble chewing. Which diet modification may be ordered?
questions.rationale: Mechanically altered textures make chewing easier while maintaining nutrition. A dental referral addresses the underlying problem.

options.text: Clear liquid diet
Mechanical soft (chopped or ground) diet
High-fiber raw vegetable diet
NPO

questions.stem: A medication is prescribed as 0.5 g PO. The available tablets are 250 mg. How many tablets should the LPN/VN give?
questions.rationale: 0.5 g = 500 mg. 500 mg ÷ 250 mg per tablet = 2 tablets.

options.text: 0.5 tablet
1 tablet
2 tablets
4 tablets

questions.stem: A client is prescribed 1,200 mL of IV fluid over 10 hours using tubing with a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL. How many drops per minute should the LPN/VN (if within scope) or RN set?
questions.rationale: 1,200 mL ÷ 10 hr = 120 mL/hr. (120 mL × 20 gtt/mL) ÷ 60 min = 40 gtt/min.

options.text: 20 gtt/min
40 gtt/min
60 gtt/min
120 gtt/min

questions.stem: Which intervention helps prevent pneumonia in a bedbound resident?
questions.rationale: Immobility and aspiration increase pneumonia risk. Movement, upright positioning, lung expansion, and oral hygiene reduce it.

options.text: Keeping the resident flat at all times
Repositioning at least every 2 hours, elevating the head of the bed during and after meals, encouraging deep breathing and coughing, and providing oral care
Limiting fluids
Avoiding mouth care to reduce stimulation

questions.stem: The LPN/VN palpates a weak, rapid, thready radial pulse in a client after surgery. What might this indicate?
questions.rationale: A thready pulse reflects low stroke volume. Combined with tachycardia and hypotension, it suggests hypovolemia or shock. A bounding pulse suggests fluid overload.

options.text: Fluid overload
Decreased circulating volume, such as from bleeding or dehydration, which should be reported with other vital signs
A normal finding
Hypertension

questions.stem: How should the LPN/VN listen for bowel sounds?
questions.rationale: Auscultating before palpation prevents stimulating bowel activity. Sounds are described as normal, hypoactive, hyperactive, or absent, and absent sounds require longer listening.

options.text: Listen in one spot for 5 seconds
Listen with the stethoscope diaphragm in all four quadrants, before palpating the abdomen, for long enough to judge whether sounds are present
Palpate the abdomen firmly first
Use the bell of the stethoscope over the chest

questions.stem: A client drinks 1.5 cups of coffee and 1 cup of juice. How much intake should the LPN/VN record?
questions.rationale: 1 cup = 240 mL. 2.5 cups × 240 mL = 600 mL. Many facilities list specific cup volumes for accurate charting.

options.text: 300 mL
600 mL
750 mL
900 mL

questions.stem: Which headache description should the LPN/VN report immediately?
questions.rationale: Thunderclap headaches or headaches with neurological signs may indicate hemorrhage, stroke, or meningitis and require emergency evaluation.

options.text: A mild tension headache relieved by acetaminophen
A sudden, severe "worst headache of my life" or a headache with weakness, confusion, stiff neck, or vision loss
A headache after skipping coffee
A mild headache with a cold

questions.stem: Where should the LPN/VN look for pallor or cyanosis in a client with dark skin?
questions.rationale: Color changes are easier to detect in areas with less pigment. Comparing with the client's baseline also helps.

options.text: Only the forehead
The conjunctivae, lips, oral mucosa, nail beds, palms, and soles
The back of the neck
The scalp

questions.stem: Which footwear should the LPN/VN recommend for an older adult at risk of falling?
questions.rationale: Supportive, nonslip footwear improves stability and reduces falls.

options.text: Loose slippers without backs
Well-fitting shoes with a closed back, low heel, and nonslip soles
Socks only on smooth floors
High heels

questions.stem: A client with postoperative delirium is confused about where they are. Which approach should the LPN/VN use?
questions.rationale: Reorientation helps clients with temporary confusion such as delirium. In advanced dementia, validation is often more appropriate than repeated reorientation.

options.text: Argue until the client agrees
Provide gentle reorientation, such as calendars, clocks, windows with daylight, and reminders of place and date, in a calm manner
Keep the room dark all day
Avoid talking to the client

questions.stem: A client recently diagnosed with multiple sclerosis says, "I feel so alone with this." Which suggestion by the LPN/VN is most helpful?
questions.rationale: Peer support reduces isolation and improves coping. The nurse also watches for signs of depression and reports concerns.

options.text: "Don't think about it."
"Many people find it helpful to connect with a support group, in person or online, where others share similar experiences. Would you like information?"
"Keep it to yourself."
"You'll get used to it."

questions.stem: A pregnant client reports an increase in thin, white, mild-smelling vaginal discharge. Which response by the LPN/VN is appropriate?
questions.rationale: Leukorrhea increases with hormonal changes. Signs of infection or possible ruptured membranes need evaluation, and douching is discouraged.

options.text: "This is a serious infection."
"An increase in thin, white discharge is common in pregnancy. Report itching, burning, a foul odor, or a gush or trickle of watery fluid."
"Douche daily."
"Use scented pads."

questions.stem: A client on postpartum day 1 has a heart rate of 58/min, is comfortable, and has normal bleeding. How should the LPN/VN interpret this?
questions.rationale: Temporary postpartum bradycardia is common. Tachycardia is more concerning because it may indicate hemorrhage or infection.

options.text: A sign of hemorrhage
Mild bradycardia can be normal in the first days after birth as blood volume and cardiac output adjust
Always a sign of infection
A sign of preeclampsia

questions.stem: A mother who is exclusively breastfeeding asks whether her baby needs any supplements. Which response reflects AAP guidance?
questions.rationale: Breast milk is low in vitamin D, and infants need protection against rickets. Formula-fed infants taking enough fortified formula typically don't need additional vitamin D.

options.text: "No supplements are ever needed."
"A daily vitamin D supplement of 400 IU is recommended for breastfed and partially breastfed infants, starting soon after birth."
"Give an iron supplement from birth to all babies."
"Give cow's milk for vitamins."

questions.stem: The LPN/VN is using a disinfectant wipe to clean a shared bedside commode. Which action ensures effective disinfection?
questions.rationale: Disinfectants need a specific wet contact time to kill organisms. Wiping them off early reduces effectiveness.

options.text: Wipe quickly and dry immediately with a towel
Keep the surface visibly wet for the full contact time listed on the product label
Use a dry cloth
Spray and wipe off immediately

questions.stem: For each food, indicate the mineral it is best known as a good source of.
questions.rationale: Knowing food sources supports diet teaching for clients with deficiencies or restrictions. Examples include potassium for diuretic use, calcium for bone health, and iron for anemia (paired with vitamin C for better absorption).
questions.answer_summary: Potassium: banana, baked potato. Calcium: yogurt, sardines with bones. Iron: red meat, lentils and fortified cereal.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old resident suddenly grabs their head and says, "This is the worst headache I've ever had." The resident then vomits and becomes drowsy. BP is 196/108 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the resident is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.rationale: A sudden thunderclap headache with vomiting and declining consciousness suggests intracranial hemorrhage, which requires emergency imaging and treatment. Aspirin could worsen bleeding, and delay can be fatal.
questions.answer_summary: Condition: possible hemorrhagic stroke. Actions: activate emergency response and notify the RN; keep at rest with HOB elevated and turn to the side if vomiting. Monitor: LOC and neuro signs; BP and breathing.

bowtie_groups.label: Condition (choose 1)
options: Possible hemorrhagic stroke (such as a subarachnoid hemorrhage)

bowtie_groups.label: Actions to take (choose 2)
options: Activate emergency response and notify the RN immediately
Keep the resident at rest with the head of the bed elevated about 30 degrees, in a quiet setting, and turn to the side if vomiting
Have the resident walk to the nurses' station
Turn off the lights and recheck in 4 hours

bowtie_groups.label: Parameters to monitor (choose 2)
options: Level of consciousness and neurological signs

questions.stem: The mother of a thriving, exclusively breastfed 8-week-old says the baby sometimes goes several days without a stool, but the stools are soft when they come. How should the LPN/VN respond?
questions.rationale: Breast milk is well absorbed, so stool frequency can decrease. Hard stools, vomiting, a swollen belly, or poor weight gain should be reported.

options.text: "Your baby is severely constipated."
"After the first month or so, some breastfed babies stool less often. Soft stools and good feeding, wet diapers, and weight gain are reassuring."
"Give your baby juice."
"Switch to formula."

questions.stem: A parent calls to say that a toddler may have swallowed two small, powerful magnets from a toy. What should the LPN/VN advise?
questions.rationale: Multiple magnets, or a magnet with metal, can pinch bowel loops together, causing perforation and obstruction. Imaging is needed urgently.

options.text: "Wait for the magnets to pass."
"Go to the emergency department right away. Swallowed magnets can attract each other through the bowel walls and cause serious injury."
"Give a laxative."
"Only worry if your child vomits."

questions.stem: A parent asks about dental sealants for a 7-year-old. What should the LPN/VN explain?
questions.rationale: Sealants significantly reduce decay in molars. Brushing with fluoride toothpaste and regular dental visits are still needed.

options.text: "Sealants are only for adults."
"Sealants are protective coatings on the chewing surfaces of back teeth that help prevent cavities, often applied when permanent molars come in."
"Sealants replace brushing."
"Sealants cause cavities."

questions.stem: At a party, a teenager has been drinking heavily and is now difficult to wake, vomiting, and breathing slowly. What should others be taught to do?
questions.rationale: Alcohol poisoning can cause respiratory depression and aspiration. Coffee and cold showers don't reverse intoxication and can cause harm.

options.text: "Let them sleep it off."
"Call 911, turn the person onto their side to prevent choking, and stay with them."
"Give coffee to wake them up."
"Put them in a cold shower."

questions.stem: An older adult with low vision has trouble reading medication bottles. Which suggestion should the LPN/VN offer?
questions.rationale: Accessible labeling reduces medication errors. Pill organizers filled by a caregiver and pharmacy talking-label services can also help.

options.text: "Guess based on pill color."
"Ask the pharmacy for large-print labels or color-coded caps, and use a magnifier and good lighting."
"Mix all pills in one container."
"Stop taking medications you can't read."

questions.stem: For which client should the LPN/VN avoid taking an oral temperature?
questions.rationale: Clients who cannot safely hold a thermometer in their mouth, or who have oral injuries, may bite the probe or be harmed. Another route is used.

options.text: An alert adult who hasn't eaten recently
A client who is confused or has a seizure disorder, or who just had oral surgery
A client who drank water 30 minutes ago
A client with a sprained ankle

questions.stem: A medication is documented as given at 1545. What time is this in standard time?
questions.rationale: For times after 1200, subtract 12 hours: 1545 − 1200 = 3:45 PM. Military time prevents AM/PM confusion in documentation.

questions.stem: Digoxin 0.125 mg is prescribed. How many micrograms is this?
questions.rationale: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg, so 0.125 mg × 1,000 = 125 mcg. Leading zeros (0.125) are always used, and trailing zeros are avoided.

options.text: 1.25 mcg
12.5 mcg
125 mcg

questions.stem: A child weighs 22 lb. A medication is prescribed at 10 mg/kg per dose. What dose should the LPN/VN prepare?
questions.rationale: 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg. 10 kg × 10 mg/kg = 100 mg. Pediatric doses are double-checked against safe ranges.

options.text: 22 mg
100 mg
220 mg
50 mg

questions.stem: How should the LPN/VN position a nasal cannula?
questions.rationale: Correct positioning follows the natural shape of the nasal passages. The nurse checks the ears and nostrils for pressure areas.

options.text: With the prongs curving upward toward the forehead
With the prongs curving downward into the nostrils, the tubing over the ears, and the slider adjusted under the chin comfortably
Taped across the mouth
With one prong in the mouth

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with no history of heart disease or stroke asks whether to start taking daily low-dose aspirin. Which response by the LPN/VN is best?
questions.rationale: Current USPSTF guidance does not recommend routinely starting aspirin for primary prevention in adults 60 and older because bleeding risks outweigh benefits. Decisions for younger adults are individualized. People already taking aspirin for a known condition should not stop without advice.

options.text: "Everyone over 60 should take aspirin daily."
"Daily aspirin isn't recommended for everyone because of bleeding risk. Talk with your provider before starting it."
"Aspirin has no risks."
"Take full-strength aspirin daily."

questions.stem: A client asks how to tell whether they are drinking enough fluids. Which response by the LPN/VN is most practical?
questions.rationale: Urine color is a simple guide. Some vitamins and medications change urine color, and clients on fluid restrictions follow their provider's limits.

options.text: "Dark urine means you're well hydrated."
"Pale yellow urine and urinating regularly throughout the day usually mean you're drinking enough, unless you have a fluid restriction."
"Thirst is never a helpful sign."
"Drink until your urine is completely clear all the time."

questions.stem: A client with urge incontinence is starting bladder retraining. Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce?
questions.rationale: Gradually lengthening voiding intervals helps the bladder hold more and reduces urgency. Limiting caffeine and alcohol also helps.

options.text: "Go to the bathroom every time you feel any urge."
"Urinate on a set schedule and gradually increase the time between trips, using relaxation or pelvic floor squeezes to suppress urges."
"Stop drinking fluids."
"Only urinate once a day."

questions.stem: A resident recovering from a stroke is slowly buttoning a shirt. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Encouraging self-care builds strength, skill, and self-esteem. Doing tasks for the resident can promote dependence.

options.text: Finish buttoning the shirt to save time
Allow extra time, offer encouragement and adaptive aids if needed, and step in only if the resident asks or becomes unsafe
Tell the resident to hurry
Dress the resident every day from now on

questions.stem: A parent notices tiny red bumps on the infant's neck and chest on a hot day. The baby is dressed in several layers. What should the LPN/VN suggest?
questions.rationale: Blocked sweat glands cause heat rash. Cooling and avoiding heavy ointments help it resolve. Fever or signs of infection need evaluation.

options.text: "Apply thick ointment."
"This is likely heat rash (miliaria). Dress your baby in light, loose clothing, keep the baby cool, and let the skin breathe."
"Add more layers."
"Give antibiotics."

questions.stem: How should the LPN/VN apply an elastic bandage to a sprained ankle?
questions.rationale: Distal-to-proximal wrapping supports venous return and reduces swelling. The nurse checks color, warmth, sensation, and capillary refill, and loosens the bandage if numbness occurs.

options.text: From the knee down to the toes
Starting at the toes (distal) and wrapping toward the leg (proximal), with even overlapping turns, snug but not tight, and checking circulation afterward
As tightly as possible
Only around the ankle joint in one layer

questions.stem: At the end of a conversation, the LPN/VN says, "So today we talked about your worries about going home, your plan to have your daughter stay with you, and questions about your medicines." Which technique is this?
questions.rationale: Summarizing reviews the key points of the conversation, confirms understanding, and gives closure.

options.text: Reflecting
Summarizing
Giving advice
Changing the subject

questions.stem: Which instruction describes progressive muscle relaxation?
questions.rationale: Alternating tension and release increases awareness of muscle tension and promotes relaxation, which helps with anxiety, pain, and sleep.

options.text: "Hold your breath for as long as possible."
"Tense one muscle group for a few seconds, then release and notice the relaxation, moving gradually through the body."
"Exercise vigorously until exhausted."
"Think about your problems in detail."

questions.stem: A client pregnant for the first time asks when she will first feel the baby move. Which response by the LPN/VN is accurate?
questions.rationale: Quickening feels like fluttering at first. People who have been pregnant before often notice it earlier, around 16 weeks.

options.text: "At about 6 weeks."
"Usually between about 18 and 20 weeks for a first pregnancy, and sometimes earlier in later pregnancies."
"Not until 36 weeks."
"You won't feel movement until labor."

questions.stem: A client at 4 months postpartum is upset about increased hair shedding. What should the LPN/VN tell her?
questions.rationale: Postpartum telogen effluvium is temporary. Bald patches or other symptoms, such as fatigue or weight changes, may warrant a check for thyroid problems or iron deficiency.

options.text: "This means a serious illness."
"Increased hair shedding is common a few months after birth as hormone levels change, and hair usually returns to normal within about a year."
"You should stop breastfeeding."
"You will lose all your hair."

questions.stem: The parent of a 6-week-old notices the baby's eyes sometimes cross. What should the LPN/VN explain?
questions.rationale: Intermittent misalignment is normal in early infancy. Persistent strabismus needs evaluation to prevent amblyopia.

options.text: "This is always a serious problem."
"Occasional crossing is common in the first few months while eye muscles develop. Tell your provider if it's constant or continues after about 4–6 months."
"Your baby needs glasses now."
"Cover one eye daily."

questions.stem: In the rare situation where recapping a needle is unavoidable, such as when no sharps container is immediately available, which technique should the LPN/VN use?
questions.rationale: Two-handed recapping causes many needlestick injuries. Safety devices and immediate disposal are preferred.

options.text: Hold the cap in one hand and push the needle in with the other
The one-handed scoop technique, placing the cap on a flat surface and scooping it with the needle
Bend the needle first
Hand the uncapped needle to a coworker

questions.stem: Why does the LPN/VN encourage early ambulation and deep breathing after surgery?
questions.rationale: Anesthesia, pain, and immobility cause shallow breathing and alveolar collapse. Movement and deep breathing reduce pulmonary and thromboembolic complications.

options.text: To increase pain
To expand the lungs and prevent atelectasis and pneumonia, and to promote circulation to prevent clots
To keep the client awake
To reduce appetite

questions.stem: For each pregnancy milestone or common experience, indicate the trimester in which it typically occurs.
questions.rationale: Knowing the timing of common changes and screenings helps nurses reinforce prenatal teaching and recognize when findings fall outside the expected pattern.
questions.answer_summary: First: nausea and vomiting, Doppler heartbeat. Second: quickening, GDM screening. Third: GBS screening, lightening.

rows.text: Nausea and vomiting are most common
Fetal heartbeat first heard by handheld Doppler (about 10–12 weeks)
Lightening, when the baby drops lower into the pelvis

questions.stem: On postoperative day 1 after abdominal surgery, a resident who has been lying in bed reports mild shortness of breath. The LPN/VN finds a temperature of 100.2°F (37.9°C), diminished breath sounds in both lung bases, SpO2 92% on room air, and an unused incentive spirometer. Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the resident is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.rationale: Shallow breathing after surgery leads to alveolar collapse, which causes mild hypoxemia, diminished breath sounds, and sometimes low-grade fever. Lung expansion exercises and mobility reverse it. Worsening dyspnea, chest pain, or a falling SpO2 would require urgent evaluation for PE or pneumonia.
questions.answer_summary: Condition: atelectasis. Actions: coach deep breathing, coughing, and incentive spirometry; help the resident sit up or ambulate and report to the RN. Monitor: SpO2 and breath sounds; temperature.

Help the resident sit up or walk as allowed, and report findings to the RN
Give a cough suppressant to stop coughing
